#10600. Android tablets are back, but are they for you?

Android tablets have always been a bit of a touchy subject, but it’s abundantly clear that the form factor is making a comeback. But, as someone who’s a fan of the smaller sizes, are you actually using the gargantuan Android tablets that every company seems obsessed with? In other words – are you the customer for the Android tablets these brands are selling?

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

For a while there, Android tablets had hit what felt like a dead end. Bigger smartphones and cooling of the tablet market as a whole, along with the general sentiment that Apple was doing a way better job with the iPad anyway, left the category in a place that felt stagnant – and that’s the nice way of putting it.

But, over the past few years, Android tablets have had a renaissance.

New form factors, big releases from a variety of brands, and flagship-tier devices left and right. Despite Android’s push into foldables and still-huge displays on nearly every smartphone, tablets are very much back. Prior to RAMageddon’s worst impacts, tablet sales were growing for nearly everyone, and Android brands were seeing a larger slice of the pie.

Anyway, this is on my mind right now because I’ve had a lot of Android tablets arrive in my office in the past few weeks, capping off a lot of tablet announcements in the past few months. I just finished up with Redmagic Astra 2, a tablet I think fits the description of “Android’s iPad Mini OLED,” and I’m in the process of moving into tablets from Lenovo and Amazon. Our Jordan Floyd has also been testing out the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra behind the scenes. And if there’s one trend amongst recent tablet releases, it’s that big tablets seem to be the primary focus among a lot of brands.

Take Amazon’s new Google Play-equipped Alexa Tablet lineup, for example.

The Alexa Tablet 12 is the crown jewel of the lineup, packing the most powerful specs and a premium anti-glare display. It’s the only one that gets a “Pro” moniker, while the 11-inch and 8-inch models are noticeable steps down. Unboxing the Alexa Tablet 8 this week, for example, I was immediately reminded this is not a premium device – the screen makes that clear without any hesitation whatsoever. It was a case of whiplash after setting up the Lenovo Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 with its 4K display.

It’s a weird one for me. I’ve never been a big fan of these super-sized Android tablets (or iPads, for that matter). I can get behind a 10-inch or 11-inch model, but I find myself more at home on the smaller slates. They’re fantastic for travel as an alternative to draining my phone’s battery, while I find myself just reaching for a laptop instead if I want a bigger screen. A big tablet, regardless of specs, can rarely replace a proper laptop for me, so lugging both around just sounds like more trouble than it’s worth.

But, clearly, people are buying these bigger slates. Samsung appears to be seeing enough success with its mammoth Galaxy Tab S Ultra lineup to keep the 14.6-inch tablet around each year while the smaller sizes are now on an every-other-year cycle. Lenovo’s lineup is virtually all underpowered when the screen size goes down, aside from the Legion Tab that’s now $900.

Are you buying these bigger tablets? What are you using them for?

I imagine that most folks opting for a bigger tablet are using these in the place of a laptop. Thinner and lighter, longer battery life, etc. And in cases like the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro and its $550~ price tag, I get the appeal. Lenovo Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 takes that down a notch for me at $799 – you’re getting into laptop territory there – but it still is a compelling-enough alternative if it fits your needs. The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra at $1,400 plus a $200 keyboard, yeah I don’t get that one at all.

Let’s discuss! I want to know if you’re using an Android tablet, what you’re using it for, and what size you actually prefer.

Ladies and gents, we’ve finally got a new flagship in the US. Motorola Signature 27 is launching on November 19 and looks excellent, though its flashy spec sheet won’t come cheap at $1,599.

Finally, something good came out of Googlebook

Googlebook is a disaster, but there’s finally one good thing coming out of it in Henry Cavill’s new “Mustache Protocol” game which, supposedly, was built on Googlebook. I’ll bite my tongue there, but the accompanying video brought a needed bit of joy into my week.

I use an 8" Samsung. Not the best in specs, but fine for browsing and reading books. I had a Nexus 10 years ago and gave it to my sister-in-law as I rarely needed something that big. My wife also uses an 8" Samsung, mostly for reading.

#10599. Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%

The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."

A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors

The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."

The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

Materials provided by RIKEN. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Customer reviews are often displayed on business websites, but presenting them effectively requires more than adding a few star icons and customer quotes. Developers need to consider semantic HTML, responsive layouts, accessibility, and how review content fits into the overall user experience.

A well-built review section makes customer feedback easy to read without distracting visitors from the rest of the page. It should also work across different screen sizes and remain understandable to people using assistive technologies.

Let's look at how to build one using standard HTML and CSS.

The first step is to structure review content properly. Instead of placing everything inside generic

elements, use meaningful HTML elements to describe the content.

For example, a review can use

as its container and
for the customer's actual feedback.

This structure separates the review from its attribution and gives the section a clear heading. The rating also includes an accessible label so screen-reader users can understand what the stars represent.

For real websites, developers should display genuine customer feedback and avoid presenting invented testimonials as actual customer experiences.

A review section might look attractive on a desktop but become difficult to read on smaller screens. CSS Grid provides a straightforward way to create a flexible layout without relying on JavaScript.

The auto-fit and minmax() combination allows cards to adjust to the available space. Instead of defining a fixed number of columns for every device, the browser fits as many cards as the container can comfortably accommodate.

Developers working with more complex interfaces can explore SitePoint's guide to responsive web design for additional layout techniques.

A responsive layout should remain readable when viewed on a phone. Avoid fixed card widths, excessive padding, and text sizes that force users to zoom.

You can also adjust spacing at smaller viewport widths:

Test the section at several viewport sizes rather than relying on one desktop preview. Check that long customer names wrap correctly, cards do not overflow, and text remains comfortable to read.

Some review components use animated sliders, automatic scrolling, or hover effects. These features can create problems for visitors who prefer reduced motion or navigate with a keyboard.

A simple approach is to avoid unnecessary animation. If transitions are included, respect the visitor's system preference:

The MDN guide to using media queries for accessibility explains how developers can adapt interfaces to user preferences.

Also make sure interactive controls have visible keyboard focus styles. A carousel should provide usable previous and next controls, clear labels, and a way to pause automatic movement if it is used.

On a production website, reviews may come from a database, a content management system, or an external review service. Keeping the content separate from the presentation makes the component easier to maintain.

Businesses can also use an online reputation management platform to monitor customer feedback and understand how their brand is perceived across online channels.

For example, a developer could store each review with fields such as:

The frontend can then render the same component for every review. This avoids manually creating separate HTML for each customer and makes future design changes easier.

Developers should also validate incoming data, handle missing fields, and avoid displaying private customer information without permission.

Before publishing, check the component in different browsers and screen sizes. Test keyboard navigation, screen-reader labels, text wrapping, and color contrast. If reviews are loaded dynamically, check how the section behaves when there are no reviews or when the data request fails.

A useful review component does not need complicated animations or a large JavaScript library. Semantic HTML, flexible CSS Grid layouts, accessible labels, and reliable content handling provide a strong foundation.

Customer feedback can only be useful on a website when visitors can understand and navigate it easily. By treating reviews as a proper interface component rather than decorative content, developers can create sections that are maintainable, accessible, and consistent with the rest of the website.

#10596. Android Auto cutting off older devices, now requires Android 11 or newer

Google has officially dropped support for some older Android versions in Android Auto, now requiring Android 11 or newer to function.

On a support page, Google says that Android 11.0 or newer is now required to use Android Auto:

An Android phone with Android 11.0 (Red Velvet Cake) or higher and an active data plan.

Previously, Google supported Android 9 and Android 10 for the in-car experience, a minimum requirement that itself was raised back in 2024 (but not enforced until 2025).

Some drivers started seeing a “Phone will no longer be supported” message in October 2026, but Google only updated its documentation this week. Android Auto 18.1, the latest app update, still supports Android 10.

#10595. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10593. Thinking of quitting your job? Don’t until you consider this factor

You know that stinging sensation you get when your coworker gets the promotion that you thought was yours? Or that sinking feeling of doom when you realize that a new hire could take over your role? Most likely, that voice within will tell you: “You’re falling behind.”

You are, however, likely ignoring an important emotional experience happening at the same time. It’s envy: simply wanting something that someone else has. Because of the stigma and shame attached to this “deadly sin,” we tend to want to suppress envy without even knowing it. It’s understandable, but also a huge inadvertent mistake.

If you’re a conscientious high achiever, or someone smart and caring, it is easy to see someone else’s success and start questioning your situation. Envy is a universal emotion. It is also normal to wonder if it’s time to make a big change, like looking for a new job or even a new career. But examining your envy first can help you avoid costly career pitfalls.

Beware of ‘Premature Game Switching’

A common reaction to workplace envy that I see among my coaching clients is to make a change. This feels like being proactive, but it is giving up on the current situation too soon, or what I call “premature game switching.” You see someone getting ahead or getting what you want in the game you’re playing. You jump the gun and assess that you can’t obtain what you want or win at this game, so you opt out and choose a different contest.

Doing something feels better than doing nothing. When we avoid taking a beat to study our envy, however, we ignore critical data.

All negative emotions have what is called “signaling value,” demanding that we pay attention to what is important. Fear helps us see danger. Grief occurs when we lose someone dear. Envy helps us see what we truly desire and avoid “desire confusion.”

Thanks to savvy advertisers and social media, we are inundated with opportunities to feel what the philosopher and critic René Girard called “mimetic desire.” We tend to want things that those around us want. While “keeping up with the Joneses” used to include only neighbors or people we encounter in real life, the blast radius for envy has widened. Now we can see many more things that many more people have. We don’t often see how these cloud our judgment.

Envy gives us a chance to see what we really want.

Heed the SIReN

To examine envy, start by looking at its four key components, or “SIReN.”

First, S is “similar target.” According to the social psychologist Abraham Tesser’s Self-Evaluation Maintenance model, we tend to compare ourselves to those who are just ahead of us, our peers or our coworkers. We envy them, while we admire those far beyond us. This provides hope, telling us that we’re not as behind as we think we are. You feel envious of the promotion, for example, because it was within your reach.

Second, I is “intangible desire.” What we truly want is not the thing itself but the feelings we believe we will experience once we have it. It isn’t really the promotion, but what it represents to you, which could be a variety of things: financial security, recognition as an expert, or the opportunity to mentor others.

Third, Re stands for “relevant comparison.” We envy in domains or areas that are important to us. If we care about our careers, we’re likely to experience career envy. It pinpoints more specifically what matters to us and where we may want to focus more energy. I, for example, don’t envy people who have podcasts, but I do envy other nonfiction authors.

Finally, N is “negative emotion.” The unpleasant feeling is a gauge. If we’re able to close the app and forget about what we saw, the envy was fleeting and perhaps not worth dwelling on. If it lingers long after you put down your smartphone, you may want to take another look at why you’re feeling that way.

Next, Channel Envy in the Right Direction

Social scientists, including Jens Lange and Jan Crusius, have shown there are two kinds of envy: benign and malicious. Malicious envy tends to occur when you’re preoccupied with the person who has what you want, while benign envy is when you focus on what it is that you want. The Right Reverend Allen Shin, Bishop Suffragan of the Episcopal Diocese of New York, recently said that with malicious envy you cede your agency to the person you envy. But when you try to figure out how to get what you want, you keep your agency.

After examining your envy and figuring out the intangible desire, the next step is to figure out some “skill-building microactions.” Ask yourself: “What tiny activities should I test out to see if I can get closer to what I want?” If, for example, you realize that the intangible desire from wanting a promotion is financial security, then quitting your job will likely become a costly error. Instead, boosting your personal finance acumen might be a better option. Or, if you’re realizing that a promotion to you means mentoring others, then perhaps learning how to get reengaged with your alumni association and finding ways to mentor younger alumni might be a way to get more immediate satisfaction.

Finally, when we can direct our envy toward meaningful work, deepening relationships and serving others, we can feel more satisfied with our lives and do some good.

#10592. Meta’s Horizon+ looks to become Meta VR+ and include 3D movies

Meta Horizon+ is rumored to be changing its name to Meta VR+ and may start including movies in addition to games with the subscription price.

Meta’s quest (ahem) to distance itself from the Horizon era is in full swing, and the latest rumor says it’s time for the company’s Game Pass-like subscription to change its brand name. VR leaker Nori posted a screenshot on X showing a handful of 3D movies coming to the Meta VR Plus service. Considering there is no such Meta VR Plus service currently, the obvious conclusion is that Meta Horizon+ is being renamed once again.

Meta Horizon+ currently includes over 100 games with its $7.99 per month subscription and is similar to Microsoft’s Xbox Game Pass service in many ways. Unironically, Meta Horizon+ also includes the basic Xbox Game Pass tier with over 50 Xbox games playable via the Game Pass cloud. Meta offers a 3-month trial with every new Meta Quest purchase.

The new Meta VR+ service is purported to include 3D movies as well, although we don’t yet know if this will be included in the regular $7.99 per month rate, or if Meta will be introducing additional content tiers, as services like Netflix, Disney+, Xbox Game Pass, and others do. Based on the screenshot, these will be big-name movies and are likely positioned to enhance the value of the upcoming $1,300 Meta VR Glasses, although all the same content will work on existing Meta Quest 3 units.

Meta has been slowly distancing itself from the “Horizon” name ever since the beginning of this year, when its VR division got a big reset. In a February blog post, Samantha Ryan, the VP of Content at Meta’s Reality Labs, spoke about the changes to the company’s strategy, including the loss of most in-house VR gaming studios. Since then, several prominent VR developers from Meta have gone on to create independent studios, including the super-popular Supernatural exercise app.

Meta then decoupled the unpopular Horizon Metaverse from its headsets, moving it to mobile-only, and has been removing the “Horizon” name from just about everything since then. Meta Horizon+ looks to be the latest big change, as the company moves toward “Meta VR” branding, which is clearer and separates its VR division from mobile and smart glasses efforts.

#10590. How to disable 5 hidden location trackers killing your iPhone’s battery

Do you always feel like somebody’s watching you?

You probably know your mapping app needs your location to give you directions. But your iPhone may be letting dozens of other apps ping your exact GPS coordinates in the background, draining your battery and quietly building a profile of everywhere you go.

Retail apps want to know when you walk into their competitors’ stores. Weather widgets constantly refresh your coordinates on your home screen even when you haven’t tapped them in a week. All of this silent radio activity burns through your battery before dinner time.

You don’t have to put your iPhone in airplane mode to stop it. You just need to shut down the unnecessary trackers hiding deep inside your system settings.

Kill precise location for apps that don’t need it

Your weather app needs to know what city you’re in, but it doesn’t need to know what side of the street you’re standing on.

Go to Settings > Privacy & Security > Location Services. Scroll through your apps and look for anything that isn’t a map or ride-sharing service. Tap each app and toggle off Precise Location at the bottom of the screen.

Restrict access to ‘While Using’

While you’re in that same menu, make sure no app is set to Always. Change every app’s permission to While Using the App.

This ensures a fast-food app or social media network can’t track your morning commute while your iPhone is locked in your pocket.

Shut down hidden Apple system services

This is where the real battery drains hide. Scroll to the very bottom of the Location Services menu and tap System Services.

You’ll see a massive list of internal trackers. You can safely turn off Location-Based Apple Ads, Routing & Traffic, and iPhone Analytics.

Your iPhone will still work perfectly, but it won’t constantly log your daily routine to send back to Cupertino.

Delete your ‘Significant Locations’ history

Inside that same System Services menu, look for a tab called Significant Locations. Apple uses this to track the places you visit most often to provide predictive traffic routing.

If you authenticate and open it, you will likely see a deeply detailed, borderline creepy map of your daily life. Tap Clear History at the bottom, then toggle the feature completely off at the top.

Turn off background app refresh

Apps love to use your location to download fresh data while you aren’t looking. Go to Settings > General > Background App Refresh.

You don’t need to turn the master switch off completely, but you should absolutely go down the list and toggle it off for social media, retail, and gaming apps that have no business running in the background.

#10589. Pixel 10a drops to $449, the best deal you’ll find after Google’s price hike

#10587. More output is no longer a sign of progress

A newborn sea turtle has a few days of stored energy to reach the safety of the open sea. It cannot afford to waste a minute on the beach. So the marvelous processes of evolution led to sea turtle hatchlings following a simple rule: Emerge at night and crawl toward the brightest horizon.

For most of turtle history, this evolutionary feature led to most baby sea turtles finding the sea successfully—on a natural beach, the brightest direction is the open sky above the sea. Humans changed that. Coastal development brought streetlights, hotels, homes, and other sources of light that weren’t the sky.

But no one told the hatchlings. They still follow the same instinct, and this year on Florida’s Anna Maria Island, volunteers recorded more than 3,000 of the tiny turtles heading the wrong way; 55 were found dead on a road in August. Biologists call this an evolutionary trap: A sudden change in the environment breaks the link between a cue and the reality it used to signal. Behavior that once worked—crawling toward the brightest horizon—starts to fail.

Thanks to AI, a wide variety of human systems are now experiencing their own versions of the evolutionary trap. These systems are being used as intended, but AI has changed the environment they operate in and is putting them under a load they were never built to carry. And the cue that organizations have long relied on to tell them they are making progress—a rising volume of output—no longer means what it once did.

The sea turtle hatchlings are crawling to their doom. Here are three fundamental issues that business leaders need to understand if they want to avoid the same fate.

1. Volume: The end of the natural limit

Human systems in business, government, and academia are being placed under enormous strain. On one leading hiring platform, the average job ad now draws around 254 applicants, and the number of applications each recruiter has to handle is up 412%. In May, the U.K.’s Information Commissioner’s Office had to issue new guidance to help public authorities cope with a rising volume of freedom of information requests generated with AI. And in September, arXiv, the preprint server where much of the world’s physics, mathematics, and computer science research first appears, received 40,363 submissions—a record, double the figure from two years earlier.

It may be hard to remember now, lost as it is in the mists of the hoary past, but producing things like job applications, research papers, and formal requests for information used to take real time and serious effort. That put a natural constraint on the volume and speed of production; as arXiv’s announcement put it, there used to be “an easily discernible, practical limit” to how fast submissions could be produced.

AI is destroying that limit by drastically lowering the marginal costs of production. It is also allowing many new producers to enter the market, because it significantly lowers the knowledge required to produce things like papers or government applications and complaints.

All that production still needs to be processed—someone has to read those job applications, evaluate those papers, respond to those requests for hitherto unpublished information. And while AI can help with this, it cannot do so at anywhere near the same rate as it can help with production, because while producing something requires only that it seem right, reviewing it means deciding that it is right.

So the final judgment—of math proofs, of job applications, of government claims—stays with human beings. And this creates a radical asymmetry. The production side has been supercharged with AI while the review side is ultimately stuck at the human pace.

2. Signaling: When effort stops meaning anything

Nobody facing a stack of job applications has the time to examine each one from scratch. They rely on signals to decide what deserves attention. But how to separate signal from noise? According to Michael Spence, who shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in economics for his work in signaling theory, signals carry information when they are expensive to send. So for example, a cover letter clearly written for a particular role worked as a signal to pay closer attention to the applicant because writing that bespoke letter took time and effort.

AI will completely destroy that kind of signaling effect. AI makes it straightforward for everyone to generate bespoke cover letters, so such letters can no longer be used to differentiate between applicants. A serious candidate becomes hard to tell apart from someone who auto-applied to a thousand jobs overnight.

None of this means AI-assisted submissions are necessarily bad. In fact, the problem arises precisely because they aren’t—it is because some AI-assisted submissions are good, and all of them are polished, that the reviewers of applications can no longer use conventional signals to quickly sort applications. And that leaves two expensive options: Either get a human being to check everything, which takes time and money; or leave the sorting to AI.

Attractive as it might be to fight fire with fire, this latter approach comes with its own issues. One of the biggest problems is that AI screeners tend to favor résumés written by AI. One study simulated hiring across 24 occupations and found that candidates who used the same AI model as the employer were 23% to 60% more likely to be shortlisted than equally qualified people who wrote their own résumés. This approach to sorting, then, ends up rewarding precisely the kind of polish that has stopped meaning anything.

AI screeners can also inherit old prejudices. Researchers found that three state-of-the-art AI models favored résumés with white-associated names 85% of the time, and a federal court has allowed a discrimination lawsuit over Workday’s AI screening tools to proceed. For the moment, then, AI cannot be relied on to separate signal from noise in the output it has made so easy to produce.

3. Understanding: Answers no one can follow

In October, OpenAI published AI-generated solutions to more than 370 outstanding math problems. This is an exciting and remarkable development. But as the mathematician Daniel Litt said, “to extract understanding from [the OpenAI results] there will be a huge amount of human labor involved.”

Litt is pointing at something businesses should take very seriously: Knowledge is not the same as understanding, and AI is producing the first far faster than humans can supply the second. Software engineers already have a name for the result: comprehension debt, the growing gap between how much code exists and how much of it anyone actually understands.

Does that gap matter if the output is right? Sometimes it doesn’t. A forecast that proves accurate is useful whether or not anyone knows how it was made. The trouble comes when circumstances change. Without understanding, a business can keep acting on a model’s confident answers long after the conditions that made them reliable have gone. Accountability is the other problem. A company remains answerable for the decisions it hands to machines, and when a regulator or a court asks why something happened, someone has to be able to explain it.

There is also a subtler cost. As Terence Tao, one of the world’s greatest mathematicians, has argued, quite often it is the process of reaching a solution, rather than the solution itself, that advances understanding. A company that lets AI do the working-out may still get its answers, but it skips the work that would have led to its next breakthrough idea.

The new scarcity

Until recently, knowledge work was constrained by the amount of time and effort it took humans to produce. AI has removed this constraint and replaced it with a different one. What is scarce now is not the ability to create output but the capacity to read and review everything that AI can help produce.

Job applications, research papers, and information requests are particularly visible signs of this shift because they cross institutional boundaries and are easy to count. But the same shift is underway inside organizations that do knowledge work. Every AI-assisted memo or slide deck an employee produces creates additional work for a colleague or boss who has to determine whether it’s useful.

No organization can give careful attention to everything its people can now produce, so leaders have to decide where that attention goes. This is, in part, a design problem.

Greenhouse, the hiring platform, now lets job seekers flag just one application per month as their top priority. The flag carries information for the same reason a tailored cover letter once did: It costs the sender something. This time the cost is one that AI cannot reduce, because an applicant who has used this month’s flag has no other to use. The company’s CEO, Daniel Chait, says candidates who use it are hired at roughly five times the rate of everyone else.

The same logic applies inside an organization. When effort no longer limits how many documents and how much code employees can hand one another for review, a limit has to be designed in, forcing people to choose which pieces of their own output most deserve attention.

Limits of this kind help separate signal from noise. But whatever gets through still has to be assessed by someone who understands the work well enough to tell the good from the merely plausible. And that understanding comes from personal experience with the work in question. An organization that hands a large part of its reasoning to AI models will find, over time, that it has fewer people able to judge what the machines produce.

The hatchlings on Anna Maria Island crawl toward the brightest horizon because, for most of their history, the brightest horizon was the one over the sea. Organizations have long treated growth in output as a sign of progress. But AI is destroying the value of that signal, and an organization that keeps steering by it is heading for the streetlights instead of the ocean. Changing course will require new signals, and people who are sufficiently immersed in the work to be able to read them and judge them.

Samsung has long left the idea of paid Galaxy AI features on the table for Galaxy devices, and now there’s finally some evidence that it’s coming and could cost $5/month.

Since the suite was introduced, Samsung has been offering Galaxy AI features for free, with an asterisk. Originally, they were only free through “the end of 2025,” but Samsung kept saying that it had no plans to start charging and, so far, has not made any announcements.

SammyGuru spotted evidence in One UI 9.5 for a new “Galaxy AI Premium” subscription. Based on strings, Samsung would be charging $4.99/month for its Galaxy AI features, though the good news is that existing features remain free.

This includes Now Brief, Browsing assist, Creative Studio, Samsung Keyboard AI features, and more.

Samsung’s Galaxy AI Premium plan would instead focus on adding new features, including:

No. I'm not interested in it. I'll do without any of that.

Samsung would also boost usage limits in this paid plan, with the sign-up screen somewhat implying that usage limits on free features could be a part of this. On top of a monthly subscription, users would also be able to buy “credit packs” that unlock additional usage for a one-time fee.

#10584. A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it

One of the biggest obstacles in quantum computing is surprisingly simple to describe: how do you read information without changing or destroying it? Unlike the bits used in ordinary computers, quantum bits, or qubits, are extraordinarily sensitive to measurement. Trying to determine their state can cause that state to collapse, potentially erasing the very information scientists want to retrieve.

Researchers have now proposed a way to overcome much of this difficulty by using an unusual electrical signal produced by the qubit itself. Their approach focuses on a special type known as an "Andreev qubit," which can generate an oscillating electric supercurrent through its own quantum behavior. By monitoring this current, scientists may be able to determine the qubit's state without directly measuring it or significantly disturbing the information it contains.

The research, supported by FAPESP, was published in Physical Review B Letters. It was led by José Carlos Egues, a full professor at the São Carlos Institute of Physics at the University of São Paulo (IFSC-USP) in Brazil, and Yugui Yao of the School of Physics at the Beijing Institute of Technology in China. If experimentally confirmed, their method could simplify quantum computing by removing the need for extra qubits used in certain measurement techniques.

Why Measuring Quantum Information Is So Difficult

Conventional computers store information in bits that have one of two values, 0 or 1. These values can be checked repeatedly without changing the information. Quantum computers work differently because their qubits can exist in superpositions, meaning they can combine the states 0 and 1 in ways that are not possible with conventional bits.

This unusual ability is central to the potential power of quantum computing. However, it also creates a major vulnerability. Quantum states can be disrupted by interactions with their surroundings, including the instruments scientists use to examine them.

"In the conventional formulation of quantum mechanics, a projective measurement causes the system to assume one of the states associated with the measured quantity. Thus, if a qubit has been prepared in a certain superposition of 0 and 1, its direct measurement tends to destroy that superposition and, consequently, the information it contained," says Egues.

To minimize this problem, physicists developed techniques known as "quantum nondemolition measurements," or QND. Many of these approaches use an additional quantum system called an ancilla. Rather than measuring the original qubit directly, researchers transfer information to the ancilla and measure that auxiliary system instead.

The term "ancilla" comes from a Latin word meaning "slave" or "servant." In modern scientific usage, it describes something that performs a supporting function. Here, the ancilla acts as an intermediary, allowing researchers to obtain information while preserving the original qubit as much as possible.

Although effective, these procedures come with practical disadvantages. Scientists must prepare the auxiliary qubits, connect them to the qubits being studied, transfer information between them, and perform repeated measurements. These additional steps require time and equipment, and the complexity becomes increasingly significant as the number of qubits grows.

"Our strategy is different. Instead of transferring the information to an auxiliary qubit, we seek to obtain it from a signal produced by the qubit under study itself," says the researcher.

A Special Quantum Bit That Produces Its Own Signal

The proposed technique relies on the unusual properties of an Andreev qubit. Its name honors Soviet physicist Alexander Andreev (1939-2023), who identified a distinctive quantum process in 1964 that occurs where normal materials meet superconductors.

Superconductors are materials that can conduct electricity without electrical resistance under appropriate conditions. At the boundaries involving these materials, special quantum states known as "Andreev states" can form. In the system studied by the researchers, these states are confined to an extremely small region between two superconducting materials.

These quantum states can represent the basic values 0 and 1, along with superpositions of those values, making them suitable for storing quantum information.

"In the system under consideration, this region is a quantum dot - that is, a nanoscale structure in which electrons are spatially confined - formed in an indium arsenide [InAs] nanowire connected to superconducting materials on both sides. It's in this environment that the states characterizing the Andreev qubit are formed," Egues explains.

The key to the new approach is an electrical phenomenon called a "supercurrent." Unlike the current flowing through ordinary electrical conductors, a supercurrent moves without resistance.

The researchers found that when the Andreev qubit exists in a superposition, the supercurrent develops a component that oscillates over time. These fluctuations arise from quantum interference between the different states making up the superposition.

Crucially, the oscillations are not random. Their behavior contains information about the qubit's underlying quantum state, potentially allowing scientists to determine what that state is without directly measuring the qubit.

"It's precisely that property that we use to read the qubit. It's that supercurrent that lies at the heart of our proposal," the researcher points out.

How a Tiny Electrical Current Reveals Quantum Information

To understand how the technique works, it helps to consider how physicists describe a qubit's state mathematically.

One common representation is the "Bloch sphere," a geometric model in which every possible pure state of a single qubit corresponds to a point on the surface of a sphere. Two angles determine the location of that point.

The first angle describes how much each of the two basic states contributes to the superposition. The second describes their relative phase, which specifies how the quantum components are aligned with one another. Together, these two measurements provide the information needed to identify the qubit's state.

According to the new research, both pieces of information can be extracted from the supercurrent. Its steady component and the size of its oscillations reveal the relative contributions of the two basic states. Meanwhile, the timing of the oscillations provides information about their phase relationship.

"Our study showed that this information is encoded in the supercurrent itself. The supercurrent has a constant component and a fluctuating component. The value of the constant component and the amplitude of the oscillation reveal the proportion of each state (0 and 1) in the superposition, and the moment when that oscillation begins reveals the phase relationship between them. Thus, by measuring how the current varies over time, it's possible to reconstruct the initial state of the qubit," Egues explains.

This means the electrical current effectively carries a signature of the quantum information stored in the system. By observing how that signature changes over time, researchers could reconstruct the qubit's original state.

A Supercurrent That Oscillates Without Voltage

Another surprising feature of the proposed system is that the electrical current can oscillate without an externally applied voltage.

Ordinarily, producing an oscillating supercurrent in this type of superconducting system requires a voltage. This familiar phenomenon is called the "AC Josephson effect."

The researchers predict something different in their Andreev qubit. Here, the current's oscillations arise naturally from the qubit's own quantum evolution. No outside voltage is required to generate them.

"Our system generates a supercurrent that varies over time like an alternating current but without voltage. It's the very evolution of the qubit's state that produces that oscillation," says Egues.

This behavior is important because it transforms quantum activity occurring on an extraordinarily small scale into a detectable electrical signal. The current provides a connection between the microscopic world of quantum states and the larger physical systems scientists can measure.

That connection is what makes the proposed reading technique possible.

Detecting Quantum States With an Extremely Sensitive Sensor

The researchers envision placing the Andreev qubit inside a closed superconducting circuit, allowing its supercurrent to circulate continuously.

Next to the circuit would sit a SQUID (superconducting quantum interference device), a highly sensitive instrument capable of detecting extremely weak magnetic fields.

Whenever an electric current flows, it produces a magnetic field. Because the supercurrent in this system oscillates, the magnetic field it generates also changes over time.

The nearby SQUID could detect these tiny magnetic variations and use them to determine the behavior of the circulating current. Since the current contains information about the qubit's quantum state, the researchers could then reconstruct that state without measuring the qubit directly.

Egues compares the arrangement to two compasses that interact through a magnetic field.

"We can think of the qubit as one compass and the SQUID as another compass. The current in the circuit produces a magnetic field, and the SQUID 'senses' that field. Since the coupling between the two is very weak, the effect of the measuring instrument on the qubit tends to be very small."

The weak interaction between the sensor and the qubit is especially important. It offers a way to gather information while minimizing the disturbance that normally accompanies quantum measurements.

Reading Quantum Information With Almost No Disturbance

In quantum physics, observing a system is not necessarily a harmless process. A measuring instrument interacts with whatever it is attempting to measure, and that interaction can change the system's behavior.

This fundamental difficulty puzzled the earliest researchers studying quantum mechanics. It remains an unavoidable feature of quantum measurements today.

The proposed technique does not eliminate this effect entirely. The SQUID still interacts with the circuit, creating a small amount of feedback that can influence the qubit. However, the team's simulations suggest that this disturbance can be reduced to a level so small that it becomes effectively negligible.

"Our method doesn't eliminate the fundamental problem of quantum measurement. But it can approach the limit of a non-destructive readout and, at the same time, avoid the use of auxiliary qubits - the ancillas - employed in other non-destructive quantum measurement protocols," Egues notes.

The approach could also remove another complication found in some existing techniques. Because researchers would not need to restore the qubit to its original state after every measurement, they could make repeated observations as the state changes.

This would allow scientists to follow the qubit's quantum evolution over time, rather than obtaining information only through separate measurement and reset cycles.

Simulations Achieve Up to 99.85% Accuracy

To investigate whether the method could work outside ideal theoretical conditions, the researchers performed computer simulations designed to account for imperfections that would arise in real experiments.

These calculations included measurement noise, as well as the small amount of feedback introduced by the detection coil. The goal was to determine whether the qubit's state could still be reconstructed accurately despite these disturbances.

The results were encouraging. Depending on the number of measurements used, the simulations produced accuracies of 99.52%, 99.81%, and 99.85%.

According to the researchers, these values fall within the standard thresholds used in quantum error correction schemes, which are designed to manage errors in quantum information processing.

The findings suggest that the method could provide highly accurate quantum state reconstruction without the additional complexity of auxiliary qubits.

However, the technique has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. The results come entirely from theoretical analysis and computer simulations, so researchers still need to establish whether a physical device can achieve comparable performance.

Could This Make Quantum Computers Simpler?

Despite the lack of experimental confirmation, the researchers emphasize that their proposal does not depend on technologies that have yet to be invented.

The calculations use realistic properties drawn from existing quantum systems, and SQUID sensors are already established tools for detecting exceptionally weak magnetic fields and electric currents.

What remains to be built is the specific arrangement of components required to implement the proposed measurement technique.

"All the numbers we used are realistic. In principle, this can be achieved. In fact, we used parameters from existing systems in our calculations. What doesn't yet exist is that geometry, that setup that we proposed," he argues.

This makes the approach different from theoretical concepts that cannot be realized until scientists develop entirely new materials or manufacturing techniques. In principle, the necessary components already exist, although assembling them into the proposed configuration and demonstrating the predicted behavior remain important challenges.

The research offers two potentially significant advances.

From the standpoint of fundamental physics, it predicts that a qubit can produce an oscillating supercurrent resembling the AC Josephson effect, but without requiring an external voltage. Instead, the oscillations emerge from the qubit's own coherent quantum evolution.

From a technological perspective, the study shows how those oscillations could serve as a measurable signature of the qubit's internal state. By analyzing the electrical current, researchers could recover quantum information while causing very little disturbance to the system.

If future experiments confirm these predictions, the method could make reading Andreev qubits substantially simpler. Eliminating auxiliary qubits and repeated resets could reduce the equipment and procedures needed to retrieve quantum information.

More fundamentally, the work points toward an intriguing possibility: information hidden in the microscopic quantum world may be accessible through an electrical current produced by the quantum system itself, offering a promising new way to observe delicate quantum states without destroying them.

#10583. Dolly Parton told Elvis no. That decision is a master class in personal branding

Even in death, Dolly Parton showed up on her own terms. Last month at the Americana Honors, she accepted a Lifetime Achievement Award through a video she recorded before she died in August at 80, a final reminder of how deliberately she shaped her own story. 

I first saw Parton as a preteen, in a movie theater with my friends, watching 9 to 5. I remember thinking it was funny and cool. I was raised to think like a feminist, and my parents assumed I would do anything I set my mind to. 

Parton proved that a personal brand works best when it’s built on who you actually are, not who others expect you to be. Her life offers three lessons for leaders. 

1. Decide whether you’re a role model or an activist. 

In her song “9 to 5,” Parton’s character puts up with a lot of sexism. Her boss is all over her, and she turns him down in a way that’s funny. Women in the audience understood. 

You might think of Gloria Steinem as an activist and Parton as a role model. But they were advancing the same cause, and it was a large part of their brands. 

Parton showed girls and women that they could look the way they wanted and still be successful. It was always about what you could do, rather than what you should do. She used humor effectively. People let their guard down when you make them laugh. 

This is a topic I explore in my forthcoming book, Let Me Introduce Myself. When you think about your personal brand, consider your strengths and passions. How do you communicate them? If you have a cause, are you a thought leader, a role model, a supporter, or an activist? 

If there’s a cause you care about at work, decide which role you’re taking because each one tells people something different about you. Then let your words and actions reinforce that choice. Remember that when you have something serious to say, sometimes a little humor can help people listen. 

2. Show up as yourself. 

Some people were surprised that Parton’s big hair, the sparkles on her clothes, and the long nails belonged to such a sharp businesswoman. She once said she thought of the music business as a business. She kept her own songs and her own publishing company. 

When Elvis Presley wanted to record “I Will Always Love You,” his manager asked for half the publishing rights. Parton refused. Years later, Whitney Houston’s version made her a fortune. 

Parton’s ultrafeminine aesthetic look told you little about her business judgment. 

Her attitude about her look seemed to be “you do you.”  

I used to tell my clients to dress in a way that reinforces their personal brand. Parton dressed the way she liked. I’ve updated my own advice. Now I say, “Dress the way you want to dress and understand that people make assumptions based on how you show up.”  

That requires self-awareness. So it’s important to know your values and read the audience. Be true to yourself but be purposeful about the messages you’re sending. 

Before your next high-stakes meeting, ask yourself what your appearance is signaling. Then decide whether to adjust it or own it, the way Parton did. 

3. Stay true to your values. 

Parton’s brand evolved over the years, but she stayed consistent in her look and in the things she cared about. 

Parton stayed focused on her mission. Her Imagination Library has given more than 200 million books to young children. Also, she built Dollywood to help the economy of the Tennessee region where she was born. 

She was in service of others and true to herself. The literacy work was her mission rather than a way to promote her brand, and her ambition served her values of generosity and lifting other people. 

Write down the two or three values your work is meant to serve. Before taking on something new, ask whether it helps you put those values into practice. 

Parton never asked to be a role model, but she used it to show people what was possible. Leaders don’t get to opt out of that scrutiny either. Your expression in a meeting, the projects you take on, and the way you treat people all send a message. Decide what you want that message to be, then live it. 

—By Andrea Wojnicki, Executive Communication Coach at Talk About Talk

#10580. Does the workplace have a 4 p.m. problem?

At 10 a.m., a meeting is just a meeting. You grab a coffee and get ready to listen to something that could probably have been summarized in an email. At 4 p.m., that same meeting can feel like a hostage situation. You’re smiling and nodding along as your coworker rattles off the quarterly goals. Meanwhile, you’re calculating: If this meeting goes past 4:55, can I make it downtown in time? Can my son use the bus service to get to baseball practice? And what exactly will happen if I’m the last parent to pick up at daycare?

This is what I like to call “high-cost hours”—those periods of the day when your job interferes with the complicated logistics of caring for your family. For parents, every hour is not equal. A 10 a.m. meeting and a 4 p.m. meeting may look the same on the shared office calendar, but they can have very different repercussions. One cuts into your productivity, and the other can derail your entire evening. Parents have always navigated this dilemma. The juggling act is nothing new. But even as work has become more flexible, one major problem remains: Scheduling can unravel someone’s childcare arrangements.


The invisible price of 4 p.m.

The real problem is not that parents don’t want to stay late. Most adults are willing to put in the hours they’re expected to work. The issue is that certain hours disproportionately impact parents, who often pay a hidden mental and financial price that employers don’t account for. Sticking around until 5:15 p.m. might mean paying for an extra hour of childcare, harassing another mom you’ve asked favors from before, or rushing home and arriving irritated and exhausted. And while you can make up that presentation after the kids are in bed, the aftercare center closes at 6 p.m. and they are not happy with you.

Parents don’t need research to understand this problem. They live it. But it can explain why it happens. A 2025 survey from KPMG found that 54% of working parents reported their work schedules often conflicted with caregiving responsibilities. Half of the parents surveyed said they needed more flexibility in their schedules. Another study from 2026 by the Pew Research Center found that parents with unpredictable work schedules were more likely to report difficulty finding childcare options that matched their scheduling needs. Flexibility, it turns out, is less about where and more about when.

Both mothers and fathers experience this stress, but because women still do the majority of household chores and caregiving, they often experience more issues with high-cost hours. They’re not just thinking about how long they will be stuck in traffic. They’re also mentally going over a to-do list that includes reminding their spouse about which kid needs a ride where and what’s in the fridge. Oh, and why hasn’t anyone responded to the class parent’s email. By late afternoon, many mothers are basically running two jobs. One just happens to actually pay her.

It’s time to rethink the clock

Does this mean we should ban all meetings after 4 p.m.? Of course not. Some meetings will always be necessary. Things come up. Clients have different schedules than your employees. Meetings will always be a part of work. But that doesn’t mean everyone’s schedule needs to accommodate all meetings. 

Managers: Figure out your employees’ high-cost hours before scheduling important meetings. Find out where the conflicts are, and ask your employees what times consistently create conflicts. Can you agree on core hours everyone should try to be available? If not, save afternoon meetings for only the times when everyone needs to be in attendance. 

Employees: It’s okay to be specific about your needs. If something conflicts with your hard stop, let your manager know you can’t make the meeting at that time. Try: “I need to be out of meetings by 5 so I can leave on time for childcare. If we really need to meet at that time, can we cover my portion first?” 

Everyone: Please stop equating staying late with working hard. Staying late means someone had to rush home or pick up a late fee. The problem isn’t that parents are less committed to their jobs as the clock approaches 5 p.m. It’s that companies still struggle to understand that being committed to work doesn’t require people to abandon everything else. We endlessly debate how many days per week employees should be in the office, whether working from home is destroying company culture, and how flexibility has ruined workplace morale. Maybe it’s time to pay closer attention to when we expect employees to work and what those expectations cost.

#10578. Build a Hardware Diagnostic Log with Vanilla JavaScript

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A device disconnects halfway through a test. The application reports a timeout, the firmware restarts, and the next attempt succeeds. Where should you start?

For developers working with connected devices, browser interfaces, or hardware prototypes, an application error is often only the final symptom. Replacing code without recording the conditions around a failure can leave you chasing the wrong layer.

This tutorial builds a small browser-based diagnostic log. It records measurements, preserves the test conditions, and exports evidence for another developer to review. You need basic HTML and JavaScript knowledge; no framework or connected instrument is required.

1. Define the question before collecting data Consider a hypothetical development board that disconnects when a peripheral starts. Several explanations remain possible: a firmware exception, a transport problem, or a power supply issue. Start with a testable question: “Does the measured supply voltage change when this peripheral starts?” That question tells you what to record and what to keep constant.

Use a known-good board of the same revision where available. Match the firmware, cable, supply, peripheral, and workload. A comparison loses value when several conditions change together.

Record the observation separately from the explanation:

The hypothesis remains provisional. A reading taken after the device restarts does not establish what happened during the failure.

2. Choose evidence that answers the question Application logs, firmware traces, and bench measurements answer different questions. A timeout establishes that an operation did not finish in time; it does not identify a failed component.

For a view of specialist equipment used in phone-board troubleshooting, DIYFIXTOOL’s overview of Chip-Level Diagnostic Tools discusses thermal imaging, BGA X-ray inspection, and inductance testing. Treat it as a vendor-authored introduction to equipment categories; use instrument documentation and board-specific references when interpreting measurements.

The log below deliberately leaves interpretation to the operator. Enter a numeric value, its unit, and the conditions under which it was measured. Do not turn an isolated reading into an automatic “faulty chip” verdict.

For physical measurements, follow the board and instrument documentation and work within your training. This tutorial covers the software record rather than a procedure for probing or repairing a powered device. 3. Build a small, accessible form

Save the following as index.html and serve it through your usual local development server. For example, if Python is installed, run python -m http. server 8000 in its directory, then open http://localhost:8000. 4. Preserve data without hiding failures

The application stores an array of records as JSON. On reload, it parses that JSON and checks the expected field types before rendering it. Parsing alone does not validate the structure of stored data.

SitePoint’s guide to looping through JSON responses provides useful background on working with objects and arrays after parsing JSON. Each table cell uses textContent, so a note containing HTML is displayed as text rather than inserted as markup. The MDN documentation for textContent explains this behavior.

Storage operations sit inside try...catch blocks because browser persistence can fail. The interface keeps new measurements in memory and offers an export when saving fails. It does not claim those measurements will survive a reload. For another practical vanilla JavaScript project, SitePoint’s **Markdown previewer tutorial **explores browser UI construction and persistence.

As **MDN’s localStorage documentation **explains, storage belongs to the document’s origin. Opening the application on a different port may therefore show a different log. This prototype is a single-browser tool, so export important sessions and avoid recording customer identifiers or private device contents.

5. Compare measurements under matching conditions Suppose two hypothetical readings are 3.29 V and 3.08 V. Their difference is −0.21 V. That arithmetic is straightforward; its meaning depends on the rail specification, measurement uncertainty, workload, and timing.

Do not add a universal voltage threshold to the application. A device-specific limit should come from its specification or an established test procedure.

If the failure is brief, a manually entered steady-state measurement may miss it entirely. Record that limitation. The next investigation may require a time-correlated capture rather than another static reading.

When sharing a session, include the firmware revision, board revision, instrument settings, and reproduction steps. A colleague should be able to repeat the comparison without guessing how the reading was obtained. 6. Verify the workflow before relying on it Try adding a decimal reading and a negative reading, then reload the page. Confirm that both values and their units remain intact. Enter a note containing test and check that it appears literally in the table.

Export the JSON and inspect the record count. Then simulate blocked storage and confirm that the interface reports the failure while allowing an export of the current session.

For a larger application, add editable entries, instrument metadata, and explicit baseline records. A shared service would also need access controls, server-side validation, and a policy for retention. These additions should follow the needs of the diagnostic workflow.

Turn a symptom into a reproducible investigation

The finished prototype captures a useful minimum: what was measured, where, when, and under which conditions. Its value comes from preserving evidence that another person can inspect.

When an application error crosses into firmware or hardware, that record helps you choose the next experiment. Repeat the failure, change one variable, and document what the new evidence supports before deciding what to fix.
