#10576. Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

Unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," says Yiwen Chu.

The breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an important role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

Quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

However, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

Mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Another important benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

To evaluate the system, the researchers tested two important computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

"The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers

One of the most significant findings is that the new system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

However, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

Chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising new route toward making those machines a reality.

Materials provided by ETH Zurich. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10575. Meet the marketers fighting AI suspicion—using advertising’s new secret weapon

Levi’s stop-motion holiday ad, “Let’s Get Fuzzy,” took 2,000 hours to create. Every detail of the spot—including its tiny sweaters on tiny horses, miniature jeans with miniature red Levi’s tabs, and adorably befuddled yeti character—was made by hand. Levi’s captured it all in a behind-the-scenes video, which is live on its main Instagram and YouTube pages. According to Kenny Mitchell, Levi’s global CMO, that behind-the-scenes component was “central” to the campaign strategy. 

“You almost want to make sure that you can show some of the verification and receipts for the hard work, effort, and craft that you’re putting in,” Mitchell says. “When we first posted our campaign on TikTok, one of the comments was like, ‘AI slop.’ And literally the next comment underneath it was, ‘No, this is stop motion.’”

For Mitchell’s team and animation partners at the production studio Blinkink, who spent four hours on every second of animation in “Let’s Get Fuzzy,” the behind-the-scenes film served a dual purpose: giving fans more access to the brand’s design efforts, and defending against inevitable AI accusations.

Recently, it’s a strategy that a host of brands seem to be adopting. Apple, Anthropologie, Prada, Dior, E.l.f., and Loewe are just a few of the major names that have recently debuted claymation, stop-motion, or hand-drawn ads with accompanying behind-the-scenes videos. As AI-finger pointing reaches a fever pitch, brands are spending more time and resources on behind-the-scenes footage, which has arguably become more important than the campaigns themselves.

The behind-the-scenes renaissance

Greg Lotus, global head of production at the creative company VML, remembers an era about 10 years ago when his clients began asking for behind-the-scenes content en masse. Often, he says, this content was more geared toward applications for advertising awards than public consumption. It lived on brand YouTube channels or on agency case study pages, where it often languished in obscurity.

“It just always seemed kind of silly to me,” Lotus says. “Nobody really cares about the fact that you had a couple days on a set and shot this toothpaste commercial.”

This modern wave of behind-the-scenes content is different for a few reasons. First, Lotus says, it’s coming from craft-forward brands that already have devoted fan bases. Second, it highlights mediums that, unlike the toothpaste commercials of yore, play especially well on film. Prada detailed how the former Disney animator John Pomeroy drew its holiday campaign “Drawing Prada” frame by frame; E.l.f. filmed the actor Alan Cumming reading narration over three adorable stop-motion characters; and Levi’s documented how it designed a tiny red sweater for an equally tiny yeti. It’s undeniable eye candy.

Notably, brands are now posting this content on their main social media pages. It’s a move that elevates the behind-the-scenes (BTS) video from an industry-facing proof point to an integral part of the campaign itself. 

“Before, BTS was something that sometimes the agencies and clients did just to have documented the process,” says Saulo Rocha, an executive creative director at Apple’s bespoke global agency TBWA\Media Arts Lab (MAL). “It was more of an internal thing, and it very rarely went to YouTube. Even YouTube is far from being what Instagram or Twitter or even TikTok can be to this kind of content.”

From brands’ perspective, the current moment couldn’t be more primed for behind-the-scenes content to hit the main feed. Mitchell, the CMO at Levi’s, says that in the era of “brand entertainment,” when consumers have ever more access to the stories that brands are intending to tell, behind-the-scenes videos give fans a way to feel like a part of the company’s design decisions. Simultaneously, the format gives brands an opportunity to prove their commitment to human creativity—and to avoid AI accusations.

“There’s been so much conversation around AI, but what you actually see is a focus from some of the best brands and sharpest minds on creative excellence being one of the big differentiators,” Mitchell says. “There’s a lot of things that AI can do, but we believe strongly—and I think you’re seeing it from others around the marketplace—that this human creativity and the craft connected to it is something that drives a tremendous amount of value for companies. It’s what our fans want to see.”

‘No slop = will shop’

To introduce its new Mac mini device this August, Apple decided to make a spot entirely using claymation. MAL, its agency, partnered with Blinkink on a 43-second spot called “The Mighty Mac mini.” As a tidbit for fans, it also posted a behind-the-scenes video to Apple’s secondary Instagram account, @helloapple. That video massively outperformed the actual spot, amassing 197 million views (compared to the spot’s 32 million on YouTube). It’s now the most-watched video ever posted by @helloapple and also one of the broader brand’s most popular social posts of all time. 

Apple is no stranger to behind-the-scenes content. The brand, alongside MAL, has always been ahead of the curve on using creative advertising to hammer home its focus on craft: Recall the 2019 airpod spot “Bounce,” which used practical effects to make a cityscape act like a trampoline park; or “Fuzzy Feelings,” a 2023 holiday spot featuring a quaint stop-motion town. Both of those spots came with a behind-the-scenes video posted to Apple’s YouTube channel. This year, though, the public reaction to the work seems to have shifted.

Take a look at the comments under the Mac mini @helloapple video, and you’ll find hundreds of users congratulating the brand. “Thank you for hiring human animators to make this,” one viewer wrote. “In a world full of ai commercials, thank you for this apple,” another said. “who else enjoys BTS more than the video itself??” a third added. 

Greg Greenberg, another executive creative director at MAL, directed Apple’s 2025 holiday spot “A Critter Carol,” which was based on puppets in a handmade forest. At the time, Greenberg says, it wasn’t meant to be a statement. Still, there was an awareness that the ad might become “part of a conversation online,” he says. It did. The spot became Apple’s most-viewed holiday film ever, racking up 141 million social views. As in the case of “The Mighty Mac mini,” much of the public reaction was tinged with gratitude. 

“Seeing brands go, ‘We know at the core what makes us human; we still believe in the creativity of people,’ that’s a comforting feeling,” Greenberg says. “I think that’s probably why you’re seeing a lot of people respond so positively. And a lot of other brands are probably making very deliberate decisions to go, ‘We need to make our work like this,’ because even if it’s not AI, but for some reason somebody confuses it for that, the internet will have its way with you if it thinks you’ve gone awry from what is the right way to do things.”

Prada, Levi’s, E.l.f., and others’ holiday campaigns certainly seem to prove Greenberg’s point. Prada’s behind-the-scenes video, which has 2.8 million views and more than 2,300 comments, is flooded with users thanking the brand for not using AI. Under Levi’s behind-the-scenes, one user wrote, “Yes!!!! Real art!!! I respect this so much.” An E.l.f. follower wrote, “No slop = will shop!”

In an email to Fast Company, E.l.f.’s CMO, Oshiya Savur, explained the brand’s reasoning for using no generative AI or computer-generated imagery (CGI) in its spot: “We’re human first, human last at E.l.f. AI can be a useful tool, but the ideas and the taste come from people. For this story, we wanted you to feel the care in every frame, because the care is part of the story.”

The internet’s general fatigue with AI-generated imagery is resulting in a positive pile-on effect for most brands’ behind-the-scenes content. For brands that miss the mark, though, the opposite is also possible. 

Dior’s 7-minute animated “Christian Dior’s Night in Color” holiday ad was directed by the French animator Sylvain Chomet, who stars in the brand’s behind-the-scenes video. In it, he says, “Technically, we work just as they did in the 1940s. It’s exactly the same technique.” But, as commenters were quick to point out on Dior’s Instagram, the ad shows several signs of AI-generated imagery. Viewers spotted warped lettering, a lazy eye, and a misplaced finger bone. The film’s creators have rebutted the claims that the ad used AI-generated imagery, instead relying on an “automated interpolation” system to generate the in-between frames of the film. Fast Company reached out to the press department at LVMH, Dior’s parent company, for comment and did not hear back.

Regardless of whether the ad did indeed use AI, fans have turned against Dior, leaving thousands of comments across its campaign videos demanding that the brand hire real artists. Right now, says Lotus at VML, marketers need to be aware that there’s a broad bias against AI. “People don’t like to be fooled,” he adds. 

In a moment when major brands could theoretically churn out an endless stream of assets using AI, audiences interpret craft as evidence of a brand’s corporate values. The behind-the-scenes video is the ultimate proof of authenticity—as long as it’s done right.

What’s next for the hand-crafted ad 

For the past several years, plenty of creatives in the ad industry have worried that AI might make their jobs obsolete. And, certainly, many agencies are relying more and more on AI technology throughout their workflows. Still, all of the creatives I spoke with for this piece agreed that as AI oversaturation increases, so does the public demand for human creativity. At a moment when advertising content can theoretically be automated in a matter of seconds, many brands are swinging all the way back to mediums that require the most human intervention. 

“There’s always an extreme to every extreme, and there’s been an extreme increase in AI and in questioning what is real and what’s not real,” Greenberg says. “That leads to an extreme on the other side, which is a proliferation of things made by hand. I don’t think that’s going to go away, but I do think, just in general, stuff always evens out.”

Greenberg thinks that we’re reaching a peak of stop-motion ads, but it’s not the end of the craft resurgence. Ultimately, he says, brands that want to develop strong fan relationships will continue investing in human-made art, whether that’s through hand-drawn animation or a live-action ad shot on film. When it comes to behind-the-scenes content, MAL’s Rocha predicts that consumers are about to become more discerning. 

“We might get more judgmental,” he says. “I think the more you see of something, the more you become empowered to critique it.” Truly great behind-the-scenes content will win out, leaving brands behind if they’re only there for the trend. “Some brands will tap into it, but for the wrong reasons. That’s going to be evident, because now we’ll feel smart enough to tell the difference,” Rocha says

Like any trend in advertising, viewers are likely to lose a bit of enthusiasm for the behind-the-scenes video in the coming months. Still, its renaissance has felt like a ray of light for many creatives; an affirmation that the public still values their work, and that brands—at least some of them—are still willing to pay for it. 

“The future may be full of perfectly generated AI content, but I suspect people will continue to gravitate toward work that bears the fingerprints of the makers,” Lotus says. “Maybe it’s the Gen X in me, but I think there’s a chord in everyone that gets struck when they encounter art made by people who cared deeply about the details. The work is great not ‘despite the imperfections,’ but because of them.”

#10572. Voice AI is quietly transforming frontline work

It’s no secret that AI chatbots and agents are answering employee questions, writing code and emails, and taking on other tasks in office environments.

But AI tools that communicate by voice, rather than through keyboards and screens, are also quietly taking off in frontline environments—from factory floors to retail stores. In some cases, AI that can understand spoken language is making it practical for workers to digitally access and share information in settings where protective gloves, outdoor weather conditions, or the need to operate other equipment have made traditional desktop or touchscreen devices difficult to use.

“With the advent of AI, voice became possible as an interface,” says Peter Moeckel, founder and CEO of Frontier Audio. “And frontline workers—they’re using their hands, they’re using their eyes for the job. That’s why the touchscreen, the keyboard, or the mouse obviously doesn’t work.”

Frontier Audio, which has raised $4.5 million in pre-seed funding, offers audio hardware and software to connect workers in industries ranging from manufacturing to aviation, including through contracts with the U.S. Air Force. The company’s devices come in a variety of form factors, including over-the-ear headphones with noise cancellation and shoulder-mounted microphones, similar to the walkie-talkie-style equipment many workers already use to stay connected. The equipment lets users talk to colleagues or AI, helping with tasks like reporting maintenance issues before they cause production problems, locating equipment such as carts in sprawling facilities, and receiving important alerts without needing to stop and look at a screen.

“We cannot add extra work,” Moeckel says. “They already have an immense amount of work to do, and we need to get out of their way. And our platform, a big part of making it seamless and enabling easy adoption is it working just like a normal radio.”

Frontier Audio is far from the only company building voice-powered AI for the workplace, often combined with radio services. Motorola Solutions offers AI features integrated into its police radios. Samsara, which builds connectivity and analytics tools for a variety of frontline operations, announced last month that voice commands have become the primary interface for people interacting with AI agents on its platform. Its voice bots can communicate with utility crews working on power lines, truck drivers arriving at unfamiliar worksites, and other workers in situations where they can’t look at a screen.

MangoApps, which offers AI and intranet-style tools geared toward frontline workers, enables users to access information about scheduling, company policies, and other matters through either text-based chat or voice in their preferred language, typically from their existing phones. Andy Tolton, vice president of marketing at MangoApps, says many businesses realized during the COVID-19 pandemic that they had limited ways to stay in contact with employees outside of traditional office roles.

“For the vast majority of businesses, their intranet is really a desktop paradigm,” he says.

While workplace AI tools have often been built chiefly with office workers in mind, businesses are now realizing they can offer multilingual access to company data and processes to field employees who, in some cases, were still using clipboards and paper forms until recently. That’s thanks to improvements in audio processing that make speech recognition and freeform conversations less frustrating, even in noisy environments, alongside advances in the ability of AI models to deliver accurate information and take action on behalf of humans.

“The speech AI technology has improved vastly, [as has] the knowledge that AI can access and be trained on,” Tolton says. “That, plus its ability to act, has increased exponentially in the last two to three years.”

Still, as in office environments, rolling out workplace AI for frontline workers isn’t as simple as flipping a switch. Businesses need to ensure that the devices workers use to communicate with AI, whether smartphones or radio-style equipment, are practical for their work environments. And whether accessed by voice or text, AI systems typically need to be integrated with existing data sources and processes for collecting employee input, while also being reliable and secure.

“In order for AI to work, you need to share data not only internally, but also with vendors. And you might also have to utilize sensitive data from your customers,” says Dayan Rodriguez, corporate vice president of global manufacturing and mobility at Microsoft.

In March, Microsoft announced new tools to build and deploy voice-powered AI agents through its Azure cloud platform. The company also offers security safeguards, including for manufacturing-specific technology that can be integrated with artificial intelligence. Microsoft points to examples of voice interfaces used by customers like Gulf Air, the national carrier of Bahrain, and electronics retailer MediaMarktSaturn, which has deployed Azure-powered voice assistants that sales employees can use to look up information about products and inventory while helping customers.

At least as critical as the technology itself, though, is ensuring that employees actually embrace it and can use it to do their jobs better, Rodriguez says. That’s part of the reason to give workers access to voice interfaces or whatever other systems make it easiest to interact with workplace tools. But it’s also important to monitor how those tools are used to make sure the investment pays off.

“Change management is more critical, in my opinion, than anything else,” he says.

#10569. We asked 4 designers what they think of Billy Evans’s Haemanthus logo

In May of 2025, news broke that Billy Evans, the partner of disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, was raising money for his own blood-testing startup, Haemanthus. At the time, Haemanthus stated explicitly on its official X account that it was “not Theranos 2.0.” Then, in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s blockbuster film You Can See Everything, which debuted in October, Evans point-blank described Haemanthus as “Theranos 2.0.”

Haemanthus has been shrouded in mystery since its inception. The glaring issue, of course, is that Evans’s plans sound distinctly similar to Holmes’s approach at Theranos, which led to her current sentence of 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. On social media, Haemanthus claims that “Elizabeth Holmes has zero involvement in Haemanthus,” while You Can See Everything paints a very different picture.

That’s led fans of the film to dig for any scraps of information that they can find about the company—which boil down to a few on-the-record statements, some patent applications, two defunct social media accounts, and one striking company wordmark. 

We asked four designers what they make of the Haemanthus logo—the only element of a brand identity that the company has revealed thus far—and their responses paint a picture of a brand that’s uninterested in following the norms.

What we know about Haemanthus

Evans has been fairly tight-lipped about the workings of Haemanthus, stating in a May 2025 New York Times interview that the company is still in stealth mode.”

According to marketing materials reviewed by the Times for that piece, Haemanthus’s device will initially use a laser to scan blood, saliva, or urine from pets and analyze the samples on a molecular level. The company’s long-term goal is to develop a stamp-size, wearable version of the product for humans, which it predicted would take about three years and $70 million to develop. At the time of that story, the Times reported that Evans had raised about $18.5 million from investors. 

As of this writing, the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office is examining the company’s request for a trademark. According to Google Patents, the company has submitted at least six patent requests for Raman spectroscopy systems (the diagnostic tool at the core of the company’s proposed technology), one of which has been granted.

Haemanthus has a LinkedIn account with no posts and an X account that was briefly active in 2025 (one of the 14 posts is just the Mark Zuckerberg quote, “In a world that’s changing so fast, the biggest risk you can take is not taking any risk”). Both accounts feature the one piece of branding that Haemanthus has made public: a black serif wordmark with an “a” and “e” that have been fused together and rendered in red. The a/e ligature (called an “ash”) also appears to serve as a stand-alone brand mark.

Fast Company reached out to Haemanthus on X and LinkedIn to ask about the design and its intent. We didn’t hear back by the time of publication. 

What a wordmark can (and can’t) tell us about a mysterious company

Given that there’s no publicly available information about Haemanthus’s brand identity, it’s impossible to know what the company intended to convey with its wordmark. However, as with any brand identity, the design embeds multiple stylistic choices, each with distinct cultural connotations, that might say something about how Haemanthus’s founders plan to position the company. 

Here’s what four designers make of the mark.

Jesse Reed, principal, Order Design: “If you were showing me this wordmark and you wanted me to describe it without knowing what space it was in, I would probably categorize it as editorial. It’s a high-contrast serif, which you see most commonly used in newspapers. It could simply be for contrast against other sans-serif grotesques that are used in the biohealth industry. There is some connection there with the use of that ligature, which is a Latin character that was used mostly in Old English. That, paired with that type choice—there’s something that they’re hinting at with this, potentially rooted in some deep human history. 

But are they doing that, or is it purely an aesthetic and they have no idea actually why they’re choosing it? It might have no meaning whatsoever. And I don’t even want to give Billy Evans any credit for anything.”

Thomas Kurppa, cofounder, Kurppa Hosk: “The red is an obvious reference to blood, but the letterforms introduce something more ambiguous. There’s a tension between scientific heritage and almost biological, ornamental expression.

Most biotech companies use design to communicate precision, clarity, and technological progress. Haemanthus takes almost the opposite approach: It’s expressive, historical, and unusually ornamental. In a field where scientific credibility is everything, that choice stands out, and it’s almost mysterious. But distinction and earning trust are two very different things.”

Dariush Aghai, cofounder, Study Hall: “A biotech company, particularly one with this history, needs to communicate scientific credibility, transparency, and trust. Instead, this feels more akin to the visual language of heritage luxury and private wealth. We know the leadership comes from extraordinary means, and the identity projects their perception of prestige and credibility, rather than what their audience needs to trust them. Founders often mistake personal taste for brand strategy. They build brands that reflect how they see themselves, rather than how they need to be understood.” 

Teemu Suviala, global chief creative officer, Landor: “When a company has such a limited public presence like Haemanthus does, its logo can end up carrying more meaning than it was designed to bear, which puts a lot of pressure on a single brand asset. We all read these things differently, based on our experience and interests. And what’s important to remember is that a logo is not a brand. We’re missing all the other elements of a working design and communications system.

A brand is also an accumulated perception in people’s minds: all the memories, associations, expectations and emotional connections built through every encounter with a company or a product. These are shaped by a complete brand identity system, products, experiences, communications, marketing, and rituals. What I’m saying is, we are definitely not seeing everything here.”

#10567. Samsung bets that you’ll either buy a Galaxy S27 Pro or Ultra next year

Samsung is teeing up to kick off 2027 with an all-new lineup of flagship smartphones, and despite rising prices at your local Best Buy, the brand is still hedging that you’re going to pony up for the most premium model available.

As reported by ETNews, Samsung is currently allotting over 70 percent of its total production capabilities to just the Galaxy S27 Ultra and the new Galaxy S27 “Pro” model expected to launch alongside it. That leaves the plain Galaxy S27 and the larger S27+ on the outside looking in. In comparison to this year’s launch, the Galaxy S26 Ultra made up about 50 percent of this series’ production volume, for a grand total of 18 million units.

Historical performance implies Samsung is probably correct here. While big displays are typically what consumers are drawn to, it does appear that the S27 Pro won’t be all that much smaller than the S27+. Considering the Pro should slot in right around the typical price point as the Plus model, it’s not hard to imagine plenty of would-be S27+ buyers moving to the Pro.

For what it’s worth, Samsung betting big on high-end devices usually pays off. We’re on year two of the Fold series seeing big successes — first with the redesigned Fold 7 in 2025, then with the reshaped Fold 8 this year — and the Galaxy S26 Ultra managed to become the best-selling Android phone in Q2 of this year in a list typically populated by iPhones and cheap Galaxy A-series models. Even with prices constantly on the rise, the people yearn for flagship smartphones. You just have to wonder where that ceiling actually is.

For most developers and freelancers, all of it lives in Google Workspace or Microsoft 365. Both are excellent tools, and both encrypt your data in transit and at rest. Here's how the three compare, what each does best, and which makes the most sense for how you work.

Google and Microsoft are built around ecosystem integration. Proton is built around keeping your data yours, without sacrificing productivity tools.

Is Proton Workspace a good alternative to Google Workspace for developers?

Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 are mature, capable platforms, and if your work depends on advanced Excel or a deep web of Google integrations, there's a good case for using them.

#10565. The solution to the data center energy crisis might be in your home

What if the solution to the energy crunch exacerbated by data center expansion wasn’t building more power plants—and investing in gas turbines and dirty fossil fuel power—but instead, simply upgrading people’s homes? 

A number of advocates and clean energy wonks believe there’s another way forward. By creating choreographed networks of batteries and smart devices, called virtual power plants (VPPs), utilities can lower power usage and create a well of excess power they can unleash during periods of high demand. Batteries can store energy during off-peak hours to deploy later, and smart thermostats can cut air conditioning by a few degrees to moderate periods of high usage. All could be paid for by leveraging the billions of dollars being spent by the energy-hungry data center sector.

“This is a bridging technology, one that can help remake the American energy system,” says Chris Walker, vice president of power and platforms for Grid Alternatives. It’s one of the nation’s largest nonprofit clean energy providers, and it’s working on pilots seeking to prove this approach can work at scale. 

“We’re hearing more and more sort of advocacy for this approach, not least because you know the data center developers really need social license, but because communities are demanding actual benefits from this,” he adds.

Home renovations may seem like an inadequate solution to the massive, and growing, energy footprint of data centers. The demand is unprecedented; Goldman Sachs predicted that data center energy use would more than double from 31 gigawatts in 2025 to 66 gigawatts by 2027. (For comparison, 66 gigawatts is enough to power more than 50 million homes.) Increasing power generation by constructing new gas power plants is costly, both financially and environmentally, and takes time; gas turbine deliveries are backed up until 2028. It’s also broadly unpopular. Americans widely rejected data center development during the 2026 midterm election cycle, when energy costs were a constant refrain.

But by using the money set to be spent on the data center energy build-out, and instead electrifying homes, adding batteries and installing solar, advocates argue it’s possible to create a distributed power system. This web of decentralized generating and power storage sites can cut energy bills, quickly create excess grid capacity that can be utilized by data centers, and build a better electrical system. It’s also much quicker to get running. These virtual power plants can be stood up in months, and at less cost.

“You’re setting up a win-win solution where a hyperscaler is able to make investments in communities that make their lives better, and they’re able to get something valuable to them in return, which is speed to power,” says Annie Gilleo, vice president of the Ad Hoc Group, an energy industry consultancy. “If we’re aligning interests with the hyperscaler, the sky is the limit.” 

The virtual power plant experiment

A number of pilots and programs are testing how to dispatch and measure distributed power systems. When proven and scaled up, this is the kind of technology that may be able to support an additional data center without requiring new power generation. 

In April in Minnesota, the state’s public utilities commission approved a $430 million utility-owned, battery-based virtual power plant, called the  Capacity*Connect program. Xcel Energy, the local utility, will work with Sparkfund, a utility services company, to deploy 200 megawatts of small batteries across homes, local businesses, and nonprofits. These will help store energy to be used during periods of high demand. 

In Virginia, Google is partnering with Voltus, a distributed energy platform, to create a 1 gigawatt virtual power plant. Announced in June and recently expanded, this system will consist of a network of flexible power assets—batteries, smart thermostats, even adjustable industrial processes at factories—that can be tapped into during times of high demand. When the grid is under strain, Voltus sends signals to those assets to either release stored power or cut usage, freeing up capacity. The system is expected to save consumers energy, and it’s being tested in the PJM grid, which runs through the nation’s Middle Atlantic region and into the Midwest. PJM’s coverage area includes Virginia, a data center hotbed. 

“We really see virtual power plants as a critical short-term solution,” Ellen Zuckerman, head of energy market development for North and South America at Google, told The New York Times. “It’s a way to invest in our communities, really double down on our clean energy ambition, but also meet capacity at speed and scale.”

And in September, Pacific Gas & Electric announced it was working with Google and Rewiring America, a home electrification nonprofit, to enroll tens of thousands of customers across its Northern California user base—and their home batteries—in a program called SHARE (Smart Home Assets for Reliability and Efficiency). Proponents argue this can cut the energy bills of participating households and create a reliable grid resource. 

In addition, Grid Alternatives is collaborating with Google in Fort Wayne, Indiana, where Google operates the massive, $2 billion Project Zodiac data center. Consisting of 12 buildings spread across 700 acres, the center continues to draw community pushback and protests over its local and environmental impacts.

The partnership is funding energy retrofits, battery storage, and solar power for roughly a dozen homes, which should all be upgraded by the end of the year. A ribbon cutting will take place on December 1, says Walker, Grid Alternatives’ power and platforms VP. It’s a very small pilot aiming to gather data and prove a larger project can be possible.

“This is 12 homes, but we want to talk about 1,200 houses,” he says.

Unlocking power that’s already there

Research shows that efficiency and grid flexibility may be potent allies in meeting growing demand and even saving money. A recent study by the Brattle Group, an economic consultancy, found that improving system utilization by 10% could cut electricity rates by roughly 3.4%; that would add up to $100 billion in a decade. VPPs also cost much less to operate.

Many such systems are already in use. The U.S. Department of Energy estimated that about roughly 30 gigawatts of VPP capacity is deployed today, and the nation could hit 160 gigawatts by 2030. Instead of spending money to add generating capacity to the grid, and racing to do so with dirty sources of power, why not increase efficiency and put the power already being generated to better use?

“We’re not going to be able to build power plants fast enough to serve demand,” says McGee Young, founder and CEO of WattCarbon, a marketplace that tracks demand-side energy resources. “How we fund and finance the deployment of distributed energy resources over the next 10 to 15 years is literally the trillion dollar question.”

Increasingly, there are policy and regulations that make this possible, says Gilleo of Ad Hoc Group. In addition, other groups have already started laying out a roadmap for where these programs could work: GRID Alternatives has built its Distributed Community Power Program on the back of work it did for the now-cancelled federal Solar for All program. Grid worked with Accenture, the technology consultancy, which created tools, including a searchable database of opportunities for distributed solar and other investments that can be deployed across Grid’s coalition of numerous partners and housing providers. The database can also help data center developers identify investable community-benefiting energy projects to support, including ones that could relieve grid congestion near their facilities.

The challenge of making it work at scale

The problem remains figuring out how to carry out the transfer of capacity. Does it work during energy peaks, and is it certain that there’s a balance of energy savings and utilization? Often, high power demand gets concentrated on a specific power line; are there enough other customers or energy usage on that line that can be freed up through these investments to feed data centers during peak usage? Gilleo was especially excited about the way the SHARE program created by PG&E, Google, and Rewiring America will study how these programs work, and within a year, provide data and insights into how to scale up the concept.

These may, at first, seem like simple shifts to the energy system. But effectively tracking the demand and usage across a real-time grid and accurately making sure everything is balanced requires extensive testing, regulations, and proof. Young at WattCarbon says that it takes a lot of convincing to get utilities, data center developers, and Big Tech to sign off on something like this.

“The lights are going to stay on because a whole bunch of random people are putting on solar panels and batteries and heat pumps,” he says. “That’s a terrifying idea.” 

Right now, as the tech industry formulates its response to the midterms and the drubbing felt by data center advocates, there is a renewed push for more community benefits. In October, Amazon announced its Built Together framework, which put $1 billion into benefits over the next five years, including energy affordability. Advocates want to see that money go toward more pilots and distributed energy projects. 

Gilleo hopes that soon, as distributed energy trials and pilots prove themselves, more of that kind of community funding gets diverted towards energy efficiency and a more responsive grid, not merely community investments. Research shows this kind of program and messaging work; a survey by the energy advocacy group Good Power found that two of the most effective promises data center developers can make are pledging to cut utility costs and use renewable power. 

 “I do think that we are at a pretty critical inflection point where we can do everything right, or we could not,” Gilleo says. “We have a really good chance to deliver a lot of benefits to communities and homeowners, but it does require us moving quickly to get the rules right.”

#10562. What working as an EMT taught Pie and Bonobos founder Andy Dunn

I got my first job the way a lot of teenagers do: through my mom.

She ran the ultrasound department at Good Samaritan Hospital in my hometown of Downers Grove, Illinois.

The summer I was 18 she introduced me to her counterpart in x-ray and helped me land the least glamorous job in the entire hospital: darkroom technician. I was a straight-up mole, developing x-rays in a pitch black room, alternating between Chicago Cubs sports radio debates on Sammy Sosa and the song “Peaches” playing on Q101 on repeat.

The easy move the next summer was to go back to that job that no one else in Chicagoland wanted. My boss liked me well enough. But even as a teenager I knew getting comfortable wasn’t the move. Instead I applied to the emergency room. The job paid better. It also required an EMT certification I didn’t have. So I took the course: nights and weekends, learning to splint fractures and say “airway, breathing, circulation” in my sleep.

That’s how, at 19, I ended up at the front desk of an ER at 2 a.m., asking a man what brought him in tonight and hearing the two words every ER greeter dreads: “Chest pain.” It can mean everything from heart attack to heartburn. Either way, it’s now your problem.

That summer taught me four things incredibly relevant to my day job as a founder and CEO.

1. Don’t stay where you started

Why leave a sure thing in x-ray? Because I already sensed something I’d spend decades confirming: Get uncomfortable, then comfortable, then get uncomfortable again. The whole point of being young and unproven is that you can switch lanes. Every move costs you something; you have to prove yourself all over again to a boss who’s never heard of you.

Startups are this on repeat. Every new investor is a new boss you have to prove yourself to. Every new potential team member is someone you need to sell. Every actual new team member is someone you need to activate, and then retain. Every quarter you graduate into a new job—more growth, more capital, more people.

You never graduate from auditioning.

The people who learn to love that fact compound who they are, and those who don’t can get stuck.

Doesn’t matter what you do—don’t stay comfortable for long.

2. Take the worst shift

They gave me the shifts nobody wanted. Nights. Weekends. Holidays. The 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. stretch when the ER alternates between zombie zones of nothingness and then a gunshot wound that wakes the whole place up.

You better be ready.

Here’s what I learned on the night shift: Taking the worst shift is the fastest way to earn the right to a better one. Not by complaining about it. Not by treating it as a stepping stone while visibly looking past it. By doing it well, at 4 a.m., when nobody important is watching.

Every startup has night shifts—the support queue when it’s just you, the unglamorous grind that doesn’t demo well, keeping the site up which no one appreciates . . . until it falls over.

Somebody has to do it.

In a meritocratic organization, the person who raises their hand without being asked is the person everyone remembers when it’s time to dole out the good stuff. Do whatever it takes. Start somewhere. Earn the right.

3. Influence without authority

Here is the org chart of an emergency room, as experienced by a 19-year-old at the front desk: Everyone outranks you. The registration staff outranks you. The PAs outrank you. The nurses outrank you. The doctors outrank everyone.

And yet the job requires getting all of these people to work with you, at speed, when the stakes are actual human lives. You cannot make a nurse do anything. What you have instead: energy, a smile, and usefulness. I made it my job to be someone people were glad to see at hour six of an overnight. I wanted the triage nurse cheering for me, not tolerating me.

Business books call this influence without authority. In the ER we called it not being a pain in the ass. Founders lean on this muscle constantly. You can’t make investors invest, candidates join, or potential customers give a shit. Early on, almost nobody has to do anything for you. Your entire company is built on people choosing to—and they choose the person they’re cheering for.

4. Quit the path, keep the ingredients

Here’s the twist: After two summers, the EMT course, and a completed premed course load, I realized—one week before the MCAT—that I didn’t want to be a doctor.

On paper, that’s a lot of wasted time. Except it wasn’t. Those summers taught me what I actually loved, which had nothing to do with Good Samaritan specifically: hard work when no one is looking, doing something that matters, and doing it with people I love.

The ER had all three.

But I didn’t want to wait 12 years to be an ER doctor. So I pivoted. Kept the ingredients, changed the recipe. Founders learn this the hard way or not at all. Some of my most valuable Bonobos years were spent on things we later killed. The tuition was worth it.

Then the twist.

Two summers after that job, I came back to Good Samaritan—not as an employee, but as a patient, in that same emergency room, with nurses and doctors who knew me from my summer shifts. One summer I was checking people in. Two summers later, someone was checking me in. That manic episode that I experienced became the opening act of my memoir, Burn Rate: Launching a Startup and Losing My Mind, and it made mental health a matter of life and death for me personally. I’d now seen the ER from both sides of the desk.

Today, as founder and CEO of Pie, I’m in the business of rebuilding the social fabric. The surgeon general tells us that lacking social connection is as dangerous as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. I’m not in an emergency room anymore, but I am working on an emergency.

I thought I left healthcare a long time ago.

Turns out I just took the long way back.

#10559. AI companies are missing a key reason people hate data centers: They’re ugly

The U.S. is experiencing a huge boom in AI investment, and data centers are at the epicenter. But amid power outages, criticisms around water usage, and moral quandaries, the infrastructure is facing intense backlash from communities earmarked for site development.

The new AI Infrastructure Coalition (AIIC)—a trade organization whose members include Google, Meta, Microsoft, and other tech giants—hopes that pledges to limit resource use, prioritize local hiring, and invest in community projects will ease the mounting friction. But all this forgets one crucial thing: People don’t want to live next to eyesores.

Of all of the millions of dollars that data center developers are spending on these structures, barely anything is allocated to their visual design. And while I would expect the largest expenses to be what they are—AI servers, electrical and power infrastructure, cooling systems, and labor—the buildings’ aesthetics mustn’t be sidelined. Far more time and money must be spent on this part of the equation.

Otherwise, AI companies risk simply adding to the growing list of reasons to resist construction. Neighborhoods are already resisting development and the backlash is reaching the leading data center locations. In Texas, for example, Governor Greg Abbott has gone so far as to implement a statewide moratorium requiring an energy audit for AI companies, halting grid approvals in the meantime. And the governor-elect, Gina Hinojosa, has said she’ll go farther, with a moratorium until the legislature passes new data center laws “to protect Texans.”

AI companies and developers will need to get creative to deal with the scale of the challenge, and while I accept that improving how centers look may not solve everything, investing more in their visual appeal would certainly help.

Because, fundamentally, people tend to view nicer-looking things more favorably. We are superficial creatures, and psychological researchers have even found that people attribute greater moral standing to animals, objects, and buildings that they perceive as more beautiful. Data centers could certainly do with that boost.

Current designs tend to have the opposite effect. Huge gray commercial units are simply not nice to look at, and economically speaking, can spark homeowner concerns about whether they’ll be able to sell their property if they choose to. Owners are already on edge, given that home sales are down, and property delistings—sellers pulling homes off the market—are hitting near-record rates. At a time when the residential market is volatile, the arrival of a massive gray industrial unit is even more unlikely to be welcomed.

It matters to everyone in the local area because Americans have a deep-rooted sense of pride in their communities, especially the way they look. The look and feel of a town really makes a difference to the people who live there, and I regularly see just how much pride a homeowner takes in having a pristine, clean-cut lawn or an aesthetically pleasing home exterior.

It is why Homeowners Associations (HOAs) keep popping up. Nationwide there are more than 370,000 communities managed by HOAs, encompassing more than 77 million residents. These HOAs set guidelines for home appearance and waste management, among other matters.

The associations take maintaining standards very seriously. Nearly half of all HOA violations are based on landscaping or architectural concerns, and they are met with penalties and fines. It could not be clearer to me that residents care deeply about these kinds of design elements—and that data center developers are missing an easy win with local communities by overlooking sites’ aesthetics.

Putting more thought into the building’s shape, ensuring the entrance has a well-maintained lawn and foliage, or making architectural modifications that match other local buildings can make a meaningful difference in how a site looks. And it could go a long way toward making residents more amenable to them.

Don’t get me wrong. I’m not saying that enhancing visual design will lead to a U-turn in public opinion. There are still plenty of resource-driven concerns that I know will worry communities far more than the building’s exterior. But, by and large, the AIIC is trying to addressing these concerns in its recent pledges.

What developers, and the AIIC for that matter, are missing is the aesthetic consideration. It carries a surprising amount of weight, and given that the leading states for data center development—Virginia and Texas—are also home to some of the largest numbers of HOA communities, it cannot be left to fly under the radar any longer.

Beautifying data centers is the low-hanging fruit that could help shift the dial back in developers’ favor. Without it, the appearance of these ugly buildings will steadily add more fuel to the flames, with communities continuing to resist construction in their backyards.

#10557. Hunter is killing Google Home, Alexa controls for its smart ceiling fans

Hunter, a major brand for ceiling fans in the US, is pulling the plug on its Google Home and Amazon Alexa bridge for controlling “HunterSMART” models in just a few weeks.

Effective January 1, 2027, Hunter will pull support for the cloud-reliant “HunterSMART” connection used for Google Home and Amazon Alexa controls. Hunter’s app and the included remote will continue to work, but connections to smart home ecosystems will not.

Beginning January 1, 2027, the legacy cloud-to-cloud connections used for app linking between the HunterSMART™ mobile apps and Google Home and/or Amazon Alexa will no longer be supported.

After this date, Google home and Alexa functionality that relies on this legacy cloud connection will no longer work for HunterSMART fans, including voice commands, scenes, and automations.

This bridge is going away in favor of a Matter connection, with Hunter having been upgrading select models to be Matter-compatible over the past year. But this is only available to “eligible” models, not everyone who was already using Hunter’s existing bridge. A list of compatible models is available on Hunter’s website, with firmware updates rolling out via the HunterSMART app.

Some models, such as the one I reviewed a few years ago, require updated hardware. Besides that, the one I have can’t even be re-connected to Wi-Fi to check for an update as Hunter’s Android app consistently crashes during the setup process.

Once the fan has been updated, it won’t be available via the existing link and will instead require re-pairing via your smart home app of choice, whether that’s Google Home or another.

…Hunter is transitioning eligible HunterSMART™ products to Matter, an industry standard designed to support broader smart-home compatibility.

If your fan is eligible for Matter-compatibility, you will be able to continue using all smart functionality within the Google Home and/or Alexa ecosystems after completing the applicable Matter migration & setup.

Once your HunterSMART fan is Matter-enabled, connecting your fan to Google and Alexa will work differently than it does today. Instead of linking your HunterSMART account to Google Home or Alexa, you will need to setup your Matter-enabled fan directly into these compatible ecosystems using the Matter setup available via the Google Home and/or Alexa apps. Matter-enabled devices do not use the legacy cloud linking service for smart controls that is being discontinued.

How can I migrate my HunterSMART fan to Matter?

Depending on your fan model and hardware configuration, a firmware update or updated hardware components may be required for Matter compatibility. Available Matter upgrade options and instructions will vary by product. You can visit our HunterSMART™ Matter resource page for the latest information about Matter compatibility, available upgrade options, and next steps.

#10556. How long-term thinking shapes the approach of Mars Snacking

Hello and welcome to Modern CEO! I’m Stephanie Mehta, CEO and chief content officer of Mansueto Ventures. Each week this newsletter explores inclusive approaches to leadership drawn from conversations with executives and entrepreneurs, and from the pages of Inc. and Fast Company. If you received this newsletter from a friend, you can sign up to get it yourself every Monday morning.

“This may be the most challenging thing I think I’ve done in my career,” says Anton Vincent, president of Mars Snacking North America and Global Ice Cream, part of packaged goods giant Mars Inc. Vincent is reflecting on the work of integrating the assets and employees of Kellanova, maker of Pringles and Cheez-It, which Mars acquired in December 2025 for $36 billion.

Vincent, who joined Mars in 2019 after a stint as CEO of U.K. food manufacturer Greencore and a 15-year run at General Mills, says the merger is operationally complex. Mars is absorbing new manufacturing facilities and dramatically expanding beyond candy, which is often an impulse buy at checkout or a special-occasion treat. Now, it’s growing its roster of savory foods, which are more likely to be on a consumer’s shopping list and come in different packaging formats.

A recipe for success

Mars leadership is also trying to create a welcoming environment for former Kellanova associates who joined the combined company, which now boasts 12,000 snacking employees in North America and 50,000 worldwide. “We’re trying to help people to understand how to imagine a future that we’re building together,” he says. “We spend a lot of time being consistent with what we think makes Mars special but also making sure that [Kellanova associates] see themselves in it.” Vincent has sought to be inclusive, creating a leadership team that includes top Kellanova executives in the combined company’s legal, sustainability, and commercial functions, for example.

There is also another tool for building culture at the new Mars Snacking: its ownership. Mars Inc., founded in 1911, remains a family-owned business. Being privately held allows the company to make investments and decisions for the long term, Vincent says. “We always like to say we don’t think in quarters; we think in generations,” he adds. “We’re in this business to keep this business, to grow this business in all the right ways over time.”

An example of that long-term approach is the company’s sustainability plan. Mars Snacking has goals for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and using more recycled packaging, enduring commitments that executives say they must consistently consider even as they strive to meet financial goals.

Changing tastes in the food sector

Indeed, family-owned businesses are playing a major role in reshaping the food sector, which has seen robust merger and acquisition activity in recent years. Consumer tastes continue to evolve, with the rise of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs shrinking appetites and shifting preferences toward better-for-you options. These market changes are putting pressure on some food conglomerates to remake their portfolios, and family-controlled companies have swooped in. In addition to Mars, closely held Ferrero Group acquired cereal maker WK Kellogg Co for $3.1 billion in September 2025. Earlier this year, family-founded Intersnack said it would acquire snack maker Utz in a deal valued at about $3 billion. In all these cases, the acquiring companies paid a healthy premium.

“Family-controlled acquirers can deploy patient, low-cost internal capital and price deals on a combined rather than stand-alone basis, letting them justify premiums public investors won’t match,” writes Food Navigator, an industry news site. 

Vincent says Mars views the Kellanova acquisition as an opportunity to grow its snacking business and expand its presence in emerging markets. He also sees a chance to increase market share in savory snacks, where Mars is a distant second to PepsiCo’s Frito-Lay division.

Leading as a humility builder

I asked Vincent how he’s changed as a leader while navigating the challenges of the merger, and he didn’t hesitate: “I think I’ve become a lot more humble,” he says. “You have to make really big decisions. And a lot of those decisions are about people.” Earlier this year, the company announced plans to relocate its North America Snacking headquarters to Chicago.

He says he is also, in many ways, reinvigorated. The merger has afforded him an opportunity to think about his impact as a leader. “Is that leadership uplifting and moving people forward?” he asks. “Even at this late stage in my career, I’m growing.” 

Modern CEO of the Year

The deadline for submissions is December 4, and the CEO or CEOs of the year will be unveiled on December 28.

#10554. Prompt Management in TypeScript: LangSmith vs Git vs 3 Open-Source Registries

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every prompt registry we tested can change a prompt in a running TypeScript app, roll it back, and give production and staging different versions. LangSmith's prompt hub, Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore all passed those three tests. The real differences show up elsewhere: which template syntax each one accepts, how many npm packages it pulls in, how long a change takes to reach the app, and what happens when the registry is down.

We tested all of this with one small app and one prompt, which has a condition and a loop. Git files served as the baseline. Every number below comes from a recorded run.

Most teams start with prompts in code: a template string, or a .txt file next to the code that uses it. That works until a product manager wants to change one sentence, and the change has to wait for a full release.

A prompt registry moves the text out of the deploy. The app fetches the prompt by name and by a label such as production. You change which version the label points to, and the app picks up the new text without a deploy.

LangSmith's prompt hub is the best-known registry, but it is not the only one. Several of the LangSmith alternatives also manage prompts, and three of them are open source and self-hostable: Langfuse, Phoenix and AcruxCore. We covered how those tools handle tracing in Self-Hosted LangSmith Alternatives: 4 Tools Tested on One TypeScript Agent. This article covers prompts only.

Every tool got the same prompt, support-reply. Its template takes three variables: a customer name, a plan, and a list of help articles. It has one condition: a priority line appears only for premium customers. It also has one loop: one line per help article. In Jinja2 syntax, the template looks like this:

One help article contains the text Settings > Export. We included it on purpose, to catch any tool that HTML-escapes > into >.

Every tool then ran the same sequence from a TypeScript script:

Each tool used its own documented TypeScript SDK. The four registries passed all six steps. The rest of this article covers how each one got there, and what it cost.

Keeping prompts in the repository costs almost nothing. The template sits in prompts/support-reply.njk, and nunjucks, the JavaScript port of Jinja2, renders it:

The autoescape: false line matters. Our first version called nunjucks.renderString() directly, and the test failed. The default environment HTML-escapes its output, so Settings > Export reached the model as Settings > Export. Escaping is correct for web pages and wrong for prompts.

Git gives you full Jinja2, code review on every prompt change, and history in the same place as the code. What it can't do is change a prompt in a running app. Every edit, and every rollback, waits for a deploy.

LangSmith stores a prompt as a serialized LangChain object (ChatPromptTemplate), not as plain text. LangSmith's own documentation says you must use the LangChain npm package to pull prompts in TypeScript (Manage prompts programmatically). So a plain TypeScript app that uses the openai package still needs langchain and @langchain/core:

Those three packages installed 23 packages and 70 MB. Most of the size is @langchain/* (27 MB) and js-tiktoken (22 MB).

Templates. In TypeScript, LangChain accepts f-string and mustache templates. Mustache sections ({{#docs}}…{{/docs}}) handled our loop. Mustache has no ==, though, so the premium check became an is_premium boolean computed in code. We also tried templateFormat: "jinja2", which LangChain's Python package supports. In TypeScript it threw DEFAULT_PARSER_MAPPING[templateFormat] is not a function.

Labels and rollback. production and staging are reserved tags, and the documentation moves them in the UI. The langsmith JavaScript client has no public method that moves a tag. Our script called the same REST route the SDK uses internally (POST /api/v1/repos/-//tags). It worked, but it is not a documented API.

Caching. The SDK caches prompts for 300 seconds by default. In our test, a running app saw the new version 300 seconds after we moved the tag.

Langfuse's TypeScript client is one package, @langfuse/client. It installed 5 packages and 8 MB:

Creating a version, moving a label and reading by label are all public SDK calls: prompt.create, prompt.update and prompt.get (Get started with prompt management).

Templates. The documentation shows only {{variable}} substitution. But compile() calls the mustache library, so sections worked for our loop. The type signature accepts only string values, so passing a list needed a cast. The Langfuse UI colours the section tags red, and it lists title and body as the prompt's variables, not docs or is_premium. We would not depend on behaviour the documentation doesn't promise. When we sent the Jinja2 version instead, Langfuse returned the {% if %} and {% for %} tags unchanged, with no error. The model would have received them as text.

Caching. The cache time is 60 seconds by default (Caching). Our app saw the change after 62 seconds. Langfuse is also the only client with a fallback option: a prompt string the SDK uses when it cannot reach the server on a cold start.

Phoenix's TypeScript client fetches a prompt by name and tag, and toSDK() converts it into the message format the openai package expects. Phoenix templates only replace variables, so the condition and the loop have to run in your code before rendering:

That is 16 lines, against 6 to 8 for the other registries. All the extra lines are template logic that now lives in the app.

Templates. Phoenix offers MUSTACHE, F_STRING and NONE formats (Prompts reference). Even in MUSTACHE mode, though, rendering is a plain replacement of {{name}}. When we sent mustache sections, they came back unchanged, with no error.

Errors. getPrompt() catches every error, logs it and returns null. You can see this in the client source, src/utils/getPromptBySelector.ts. A missing prompt and an unreachable server look the same to your code, which is why the snippet checks for null.

Size and caching. The client installed 57 packages and 90 MB. Most of that is OpenTelemetry, which comes in through its @arizeai/phoenix-otel dependency. The client has no prompt cache, so every render is a network call. That is also why a label change showed up immediately: 0 seconds in our test.

AcruxCore stores Jinja2 templates and renders them on the server with nunjucks. The SDK sends the variables and gets back finished messages:

The template from the test section works as it is, condition and loop included, with no is_premium flag computed in code. A label is called an alias here, and promoteAlias() moves it (Manage prompts via the SDK). The SDK installed 3 packages and 12 MB. Most of the 12 MB is one OpenTelemetry package, @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions.

Templates. Jinja2 only. When we committed the mustache version, AcruxCore rejected it at commit time with Template parse error: unexpected token: #. That is a clear error, but it also means that moving mustache prompts from LangSmith or Langfuse requires rewriting them.

We sent the same two templates, a Jinja2 one and a mustache one, to each tool's own renderer:

The rows that matter most are the ones where the tags were left in the output, because those failures produce no error. The model receives raw template syntax, and the only symptom is a strange answer. Whatever tool you pick, test one prompt with logic in it before you move the rest.

Putting logic in the template is not automatically better. It lets someone change the condition without a deploy. It also lets them break the condition without a deploy. Keeping logic in code, as Phoenix forces you to do, puts every branch under code review and in your tests.

A registry is a new runtime dependency, so we tested an outage. The app reached each registry through a local proxy, and we switched the proxy off. A separate process then started while the registry was still unreachable.

LangSmith, Langfuse and AcruxCore keep serving the last good version while the registry is down, even after the cache time has passed. The risk is a cold start: a new container or a serverless function that boots during the outage. Langfuse's fallback option is the built-in answer to that. With the other tools, keep a copy of each prompt in your code as a fallback, which brings back part of the Git setup.

Keep prompts in Git if engineers make every prompt change and your deploys are quick. Set autoescape: false, and you get Jinja2, reviews and history for free.

Use LangSmith's prompt hub if you already use LangChain, or already trace with LangSmith. If your app doesn't use LangChain, budget for the extra dependency and for the tag moves that only the UI supports.

Use Langfuse if you want a small client, a local compile(), and a fallback for cold starts. Keep to {{variable}} substitution unless you are comfortable relying on mustache behaviour that the documentation doesn't promise.

Use Phoenix if you already use it for tracing, or if you prefer all template logic in code. Remember the null check, and that every render is a network call.

Use AcruxCore if you want real conditions and loops in the template and rendering on the server. Expect one network call per new set of variables, and a personal API key for writes.

Before you choose, run one of your own prompts with real logic in it through the tool's SDK, not through its playground. Two of the four registries we tested failed on template syntax without any error, and an SDK run is where you would see that.

#10553. Googlebook apps built by Googlers add macOS-like status bar shortcuts, keyboard commands

Googlebooks are a bit starved of desktop-class features at launch, but one of Google’s pitches around this platform is how apps can be built for it, and the company’s own employees are showing off what that looks like with some clever apps that just so happen to add features that feel a lot like they’re replicating macOS staples.

In a Reddit thread, three Googlebook apps built by Googlers through Antigravity are shown off, and they’re pretty cool, regardless of how you might feel about the platform itself.

“BentoBox” is a utility that gives you control over the status bar on Googlebook, enabling you to fill the status bar with shortcuts, mini-apps, and more. It’s full of glancable information such as weather conditions, battery charging speeds, and more, but also includes useful tools such as being able to access a clipboard history, set a timer, and more. The app requires permissions including accessibility overlays, but it works like a charm.

I had no idea the status bar on Googlebook could even be used like this, and it really makes that space a lot more useful. Of course, you have to draw a comparison here to macOS, which also uses this space for app shortcuts and tools, though BentoBox offers a different type of customization.

BentoBox is available for download via Google Play for free.

The other Mac-like app here is “Booklight,” a launcher that’s basically Apple’s Spotlight, just for Googlebook. It has a transparent design and lets you search “apps, settings, and the web.”

Technically, Googlebook already can do this in its built-in search bar (in the app drawer), but Booklight has more customization and functionality, including being able to write out shorthand commands all in one sentence with the app then completing the command in the appropriate apps, as well as having a clearer UI for experiences such as typing in quick math equations. It’s also good at finding symbols (so you don’t have to remember the U+ codes that carried over from ChromeOS). Not one I found myself wanting to use, but the potential is there.

Both BentoBox and Booklight were developed by Alexander Kuscher, VP over Laptops & Tablets at Google.

The other app highlighted in Google’s thread was Wayfinder, a file manager app described as a “desktop-grade file manager.” The big bonus here is network file access for NAS boxes and other uses, but the app also just has a more advanced UX compared to Googlebook’s built-in Files app.

Googlebook’s app gap is a real problem at launch, but these apps do show there’s a lot of potential in the platform, it’s just a matter of getting developers on board – which itself will require Google and its partners to actually sell some of these laptops… classic chicken-and-egg situation.
